design_detail: Short report (BMJ 'Papers', two pages) of a follow-up study: 137 consecutive people dependent on opiates admitted for detoxification within a 28-day inpatient programme at one London unit, followed for 12 months after discharge for vital status, with interviews at a mean of 8.7 months. People were grouped by how far they got through treatment and labelled by the tolerance the authors presume they had at discharge: failed to complete detoxification ('still tolerant', 43), completed detoxification but left the programme early ('reduced tolerance', 57), completed detoxification and the whole programme ('lost tolerance', 37). Deaths and their causes were compared across groups, and the characteristics of the 5 who died were compared with those of the other 132. Tolerance was not measured and nothing was adjusted.
can_establish: That in this small cohort all three overdose deaths in the year after discharge occurred among the 37 people who completed both detoxification and the full programme, within four months of leaving, and none among the 100 who left earlier.
cannot_establish: That loss of tolerance caused these deaths (tolerance was not measured, there were only 3 overdose deaths, and the groups and the people who died differed in other ways), or how large the excess risk of overdose after detoxification is in general.

sample.recruitment: Treatment-seeking: consecutive people dependent on opiates receiving detoxification within a 28-day inpatient treatment programme, recruited over 20 months, who consented to follow-up (p. 959). The acknowledgments name the unit as Wickham Park House, Bethlem Royal Hospital, South London and Maudsley NHS Trust (p. 960). Dates of recruitment are not given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Detoxification within the inpatient programme and consent to follow-up; no other criteria are reported.
sample.demographics: The 5 who died were all men, mean age 31.4 (SD 7.1); of the other 132, 75% were men, mean age 32.6 (SD 7.3); 70% of the 132 had had previous inpatient treatment and 39% (of 130) had ever overdosed (Table, p. 959). Ethnicity, injecting and other drug use are not reported.
sample.attrition: Vital status was known for all 137 at one year: 5 died, 103 were interviewed (mean 8.7 months after discharge) and a records search showed the other 29 alive one year after discharge (pp. 959–960). Interview data are missing for 29 of the 132 survivors (22%).
sample.selection_effects: One inpatient unit; consent-based (the number who declined is not reported). Group membership depends on behaviour during treatment (completing detoxification, staying for the programme), which may itself reflect motivation, social circumstances and later drug use. The people who died differed from the others in living alone (80% vs 16%), methadone dose before admission and days of heroin use.

exposure.measurement: Tolerance was not measured. The three groups were defined from treatment records of completing detoxification and the programme, and labelled by the tolerance the authors presume each would have on leaving (p. 960, Participants, methods, and results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Month before admission (Table, p. 959): all 5 who died and 92 of the other 132 (70%) were prescribed methadone; mean prescribed methadone dose 51.0 mg (SD 20.7) in those who died vs 29.2 mg (SD 23.1) in the others; mean days of heroin use 14.4 (SD 14.4) vs 24.5 (SD 10.2). The detoxification regimen is not described.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: no data on alcohol, benzodiazepines or other drugs before or after discharge.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not measured at discharge. Drug use after discharge is not reported, except that both deaths not due to overdose were in people who had relapsed.

comparison.controls: Internal comparisons only: across the three completion groups, and between the 5 who died and the other 132 (Table). External comparison only as an expectation from earlier published data (one or two deaths in a year, one from overdose).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance at discharge, drug use and return to treatment after discharge, use of other depressant drugs, and the circumstances of the deaths (for example whether anyone was present) were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Death within 12 months of discharge and its cause (the source of cause-of-death information is not stated); a records search for the vital status of people not interviewed; the Maudsley Addiction Profile (MAP) physical health score.
outcomes.validity_norms: Death is a hard outcome; how overdose was established as the cause (coroner, death certificate, toxicology) is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Death, and death from overdose, within 12 months of discharge; all three overdose deaths occurred within the first four months.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Twelve characteristics were compared between the 5 who died and the other 132 (Table), five with P<0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to vital status; not reported for the cause of death.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts. Deaths within 12 months: lost-tolerance group 4 of 37 (3 overdoses, 1 end-stage renal failure), reduced-tolerance group 1 of 57 (Clostridium welchii infection), still-tolerant group 0 of 43; Fisher's exact test P=0.02 (p. 960). Editors' calculations (exact binomial 95% CIs): overdose deaths 3/37, 8.1% (1.7% to 21.9%) in the lost-tolerance group, against 0/100 (0% to 3.6%) in the two other groups combined and 3/94, 3.2% (0.7% to 9.0%) among everyone who completed detoxification. A Fisher–Freeman–Halton test on the printed counts gives P=0.021 for all deaths (0, 1, 4) and P=0.019 for overdose deaths (0, 0, 3), so the printed P=0.02 fits either. Against the authors' expectation of one or two deaths and one overdose death, the Poisson probability of 5 or more deaths is 0.02 to 0.05 and of 3 or more overdose deaths 0.08 (editors' calculation). The 5 who died vs the other 132 (Table, p. 959): living alone 80% vs 16% (Fisher P=0.004); prescribed methadone dose 51.0 vs 29.2 mg (t=2.08, P=0.04); days of heroin use 14.4 vs 24.5 (t=2.15, P=0.03); inpatient stay 24.6 vs 15.6 days (t=2.44, P=0.02); completed the full programme 80% vs 25% (P=0.02).
analysis.covariates: None; with 5 deaths no adjusted analysis was possible.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is cited. The contributors' statement says the first author conceived this analysis of data from a follow-up study designed by four of the authors (p. 960).
analysis.selective_reporting: The tolerance grouping and the comparison of the 5 deaths with the rest are presented as an analysis conceived from a wider follow-up study; other outcomes of that study are not reported here.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 3 overdose deaths only a very large clustering could be detected, and every interval is wide.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Three overdose deaths, all within four months of discharge and all among the 37 people who completed detoxification and the full programme; no overdose death among the 100 who left earlier; the 5 people who died had more often lived alone, had been prescribed higher methadone doses and had used heroin on fewer days before admission.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and comment attribute the deaths to loss of tolerance, calling the clustering "counterintuitive and illogical—unless it derives from loss of tolerance" (p. 960), though tolerance was never measured. The 57 people who completed detoxification but left the programme early (presumed reduced tolerance) had no overdose death, so the tolerance gradient rests on 3 deaths. The characteristics of those who died (living alone, higher methadone dose, fewer heroin days) are offered as possible clinical markers of risk, not examined as alternative explanations. The authors do say that the study urgently requires replication (p. 960).

timeline.event: Capelhorn (spelling as printed): deaths in the first two weeks of methadone treatment in New South Wales, 1994, cited for the transient rise in deaths at the start of methadone treatment (ref. 2, p. 959).

Bird & Hutchinson: drug-related deaths of men in the fortnight after release from prison, Scotland 1996–99, cited with ref. 1 for the attribution of excess deaths after release to loss of tolerance and misjudged dose (ref. 3, p. 959).
This study: 3 overdose deaths, all among people who completed inpatient detoxification and the full programme.

Sordo et al. meta-analysis of cohorts in methadone or buprenorphine maintenance (detoxification excluded): all-cause mortality of 32.1 per 1000 person-years in the first four weeks after leaving methadone treatment vs 13.5 later

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no direct replication after inpatient detoxification was among the papers read for this card. The finding is a signal from 3 deaths in one unit, consistent in direction with the higher mortality reported after leaving opioid maintenance treatment (Sordo et al., 2017) and with the excess deaths after prison release that both papers cite, but it does not show how much risk rises after detoxification or that loss of tolerance is the reason.

funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the National Addiction Centre (Institute of Psychiatry and the Maudsley Hospital, London); the unit studied belongs to the South London and Maudsley NHS Trust. Ethical approval: South London and Maudsley ethical committee. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A larger, multi-site cohort of people leaving inpatient or residential detoxification, linked to death registers, with markers of tolerance at discharge (days without opioids, toxicology), drug use and return to treatment recorded after discharge, enough deaths for adjusted comparisons (including living alone and use of other depressant drugs), and a comparison group continuing maintenance treatment.

domains.note: No adjustment was possible with 5 deaths. Completing treatment is self-selected, and the people who died differed in living alone (80% vs 16%), prescribed methadone dose and days of heroin use.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Consecutive admissions who consented; refusals are not reported. Follow-up starts at discharge in every group, so there is no immortal time.
The groups are clearly defined from treatment records, but they are labelled by tolerance levels that were never measured.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: What happened after discharge (aftercare, return to methadone, relapse) is not reported, except that the two deaths not due to overdose followed relapse.
Death is objective, but the source used to classify a death as overdose is not stated.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; the tolerance grouping and the comparison of those who died with the rest are presented as an analysis conceived from a wider follow-up study.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because the groups compared are defined by how much of an intervention (inpatient detoxification and the 28-day programme) people completed; the paper's exposure of interest, loss of tolerance, is inferred from that completion and never measured. The clustering of 3 overdose deaths among people who completed treatment is a real signal in this cohort, but with no adjustment, no measure of tolerance and 3 events it cannot separate loss of tolerance from other differences (living alone, earlier methadone dose) or from chance. Cite it, with its numbers, as an early small signal that the months after completing detoxification can carry a high risk of overdose death, not as a measure of that risk.

key_findings.finding: 137 consecutive people dependent on opiates, admitted for detoxification within a 28-day inpatient programme and recruited over 20 months, were followed for 12 months after discharge; vital status was known for all (5 died; 103 were interviewed at a mean of 8.7 months; records showed the other 29 alive at one year).
key_findings.locator: Participants, methods, and results, 1st paragraph (begins p. 959, middle column; continues p. 960, left column)

key_findings.finding: Groups at discharge: 43 failed to complete detoxification ('still tolerant'); 57 completed the prescribed detoxification but left the programme early ('reduced tolerance'); 37 completed detoxification and the whole inpatient programme ('lost tolerance').

Five people died within 12 months of discharge. Three died of an overdose, all within the first four months and all in the lost-tolerance group. The two other deaths, in people who had relapsed, were one in the lost-tolerance group (end-stage renal failure) and one in the reduced-tolerance group (Clostridium welchii infection). No one in the still-tolerant group died (Fisher's exact test, P=0.02).
key_findings.locator: Participants, methods, and results, 1st paragraph (p. 960 part) and 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: overdose deaths 3/37 (8.1%, exact 95% CI 1.7% to 21.9%) vs 0/100 (0% to 3.6%) in the two other groups; the printed P=0.02 matches a 2×3 exact test on either all deaths or overdose deaths.

key_findings.finding: The clustering was not explained by time to the follow-up interview: mean 9.5 months in the still-tolerant, 8.7 in the reduced-tolerance and 7.8 in the lost-tolerance group.

The 5 who died (all men) vs the other 132: living alone in the month before admission 4 (80%) vs 21 of 130 (16%), P=0.004; prescribed methadone dose 51.0 mg (SD 20.7) vs 29.2 mg (SD 23.1), P=0.04; days of heroin use in the month before admission 14.4 (SD 14.4) vs 24.5 (SD 10.2), P=0.03; length of inpatient stay 24.6 (SD 7.6) vs 15.6 (SD 8.1) days, P=0.02; completed the full programme 80% vs 25%, P=0.02. Age, sex, previous inpatient treatment, ever having overdosed, being prescribed methadone, MAP physical health and completing detoxification did not differ significantly.
key_findings.locator: Table (Predictors of mortality among patients who underwent inpatient opiate detoxification); also p. 960, Participants, methods, and results, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The 5 deaths include 2 not due to overdose; twelve comparisons were made without correction. Whether the other patients' mean methadone dose is averaged over the 92 prescribed methadone or over all 132 is not stated.

key_findings.finding: From earlier published data, the authors would have expected only one or two deaths within a year in a group this size, and only one from overdose.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with one or two deaths expected, the Poisson probability of 5 or more is 0.02 to 0.05; with one overdose death expected, the probability of 3 or more is 0.08.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the study urgently requires replication and that, if confirmed, the finding must be addressed in inpatient, residential, custodial and aftercare programmes.

Context given in the introduction: treatment reduces mortality but can transiently increase it, for example in the first weeks of methadone treatment and after release from prison, where the excess has been attributed to loss of tolerance and misjudged dose on return to opiate use.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded, one paragraph, left and middle columns)

reporting_issues.issue: 'Ever overdosed' among the other patients is printed as 50 (39%) of 130; 50 of 130 is 38.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding slip; no effect on interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: Fisher's exact test is reported with 'df=2', and the text does not say whether it compares all deaths or overdose deaths across the three groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both comparisons give P≈0.02 (editors' calculation), so the conclusion is unchanged, but the test covers 5 deaths in one reading and 3 in the other.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table compares all 5 deaths, including 2 not due to overdose, with the other 132 patients, although the paper's question is overdose after loss of tolerance.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'clinical markers' describe 5 deaths of any cause and cannot be read as markers of overdose risk.

reporting_issues.issue: The groups are labelled 'still tolerant', 'reduced tolerance' and 'lost tolerance', but no measure of tolerance or of opioid use at discharge is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should describe the groups by what people did (completed detoxification, completed the programme), not by tolerance.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), pp. 959–960 (the whole article; the table and text checked on rendered pages at 150 and 300 dpi; the same PDF pages also carry the end of the preceding and the start of the following BMJ article, not read; no supplement)
